newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine grain crop escapes flood damage.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine grain crop escapes flood damage.

text.p: Flooding in central and eastern Europe has not threatened grain crops in Ukraine, but dry weather is needed for crops to flourish, analysts said on Tuesday.
Sunshine and minor isolated showers are forecast over the next week to help Ukraine achieve its harvest target of 37 million tonnes.
"Ten hot, sunny days would be just what they need," said Stephan von Cramon Taubadel, an agricultural expert with the German Advisory Group on Economic Reforms of Ukraine.
"Year on year they are a good two weeks behind (with harvesting)", he said. "But last year it was dry and they were early, so it doesn't mean they're that late this year."
Poland, the Czech Republic and eastern Germany have experienced some of the worse flooding this century, resulting in the deaths of about 100 people and crop damage.
Western Ukraine's Lviv region, which borders Poland, reported heavy rains and some flooding at the weekend -- but the hilly area is not traditionally given to large amounts of grain growing.
Ukraine's grain harvest is in full swing, but started later this year because fields were too wet to harvest after higher-than-normal rains at the start of July.
"The weather still is a danger," Taubadel said. "They need sun to get the machines going in the fields."
He said weeds that had sprouted because of the rains could also clog up combines.
Most Ukrainian farms operate with old and inefficient Soviet-era machines.
Taubadel said that even if Ukraine harvested grain quickly, it still lacked the infrastructure to get the grain to market rapidly, which could mean a drop in grain quality due to moisture problems.
"They might get a glut and that would bring prices down," he said.
Many of Ukraine's elevators lack proper drying and storage facilities to prevent grain spoilage.

Olexandr Kotyash, chief agronomist of the Lviv regional administration in western Ukraine, said by telephone that Ukraine might have lost 60,000 tonnes, mostly wheat, when several rivers overran their banks following heavy rains at the weekend.
"Only small areas were damaged," he said. "We think this is probably the end of the rains."

Western experts have said Ukraine's sugar beet output, forecast this year at 27 million tonnes against 24 million tonnes last year, could benefit from the rains. They have also said the barley crop could do better than last year's 5.7 million tonnes.
